questions.question: A Linux administrator needs to add a kernel module for a new network card without rebooting the system. The module is called 'e1000e'. Which command accomplishes this?
questions.explanation: modprobe is the correct tool for loading kernel modules because it automatically resolves and loads any module dependencies. insmod can load a module but requires the full path to the .ko file and does not handle dependencies. modinfo only displays information about a module without loading it. lsmod lists currently loaded modules but does not load new ones.

questions.question: After a power failure, a server boots into emergency mode with the message 'Failed to mount /data'. The /data partition uses ext4. Which command should the administrator run first to recover the filesystem?
questions.explanation: e2fsck -f forces a filesystem check on an ext4 partition even if it appears clean, which is appropriate after an unclean shutdown. fsck -y would work but -y auto-answers yes to all prompts which can be risky. mount -o remount,rw will fail if the filesystem has errors. xfs_repair is only for XFS filesystems, not ext4.

questions.question: A sysadmin wants a new systemd service called 'appd' to start automatically at multi-user.target. Which directive in the [Install] section of the unit file is required?
questions.explanation: WantedBy=multi-user.target in the [Install] section causes systemctl enable to create a symlink in multi-user.target.wants/, making the service start at that target. RequiredBy is not a standard [Install] directive. After= and Requires= belong in [Unit] and control ordering/dependencies but do not enable autostart.

questions.question: An administrator needs to create a 10 GB logical volume named 'datalv' in a volume group named 'datavg'. Which command is correct?
questions.explanation: lvcreate -L 10G -n datalv datavg creates a 10 GB logical volume named datalv in the datavg volume group. The -L flag specifies size and -n specifies the name. lvcreate -s creates a snapshot, not a regular LV. vgcreate creates a volume group from physical volumes, not logical volumes. pvcreate initializes a physical volume and does not accept -n or -L in this way.

questions.question: A user account 'jsmith' needs to be locked immediately without deleting the account or its data. Which command achieves this?
questions.explanation: usermod -L locks the account by prepending '!' to the password hash in /etc/shadow, preventing password-based login. userdel -r deletes the account and home directory. passwd -e forces the user to change their password at next login rather than locking the account. chage -I -1 sets the inactivity period but does not immediately lock the account.

questions.question: A system is configured with UEFI firmware. During boot, the administrator needs to interrupt the GRUB2 menu to boot an older kernel. Which file contains the GRUB2 menu timeout setting?
questions.explanation: /etc/default/grub contains the GRUB_TIMEOUT and other configurable settings that are used as input by grub2-mkconfig to generate grub.cfg. The grub.cfg file is auto-generated and should not be edited directly. /etc/grub.d/40_custom is used for adding custom menu entries. grubenv stores boot environment variables like the saved default entry.

questions.question: An administrator runs 'chage -l alice' and sees 'Password expires: Mar 01, 2026'. It is currently April. Alice can still log in with her password. What is the most likely reason?
options: The /etc/shadow file has a different expiry than chage reports
PAM is configured to ignore password expiry on this system
The account has INACTIVE days set to a high value allowing grace logins
Alice's SSH key authentication bypasses password expiry checks
questions.explanation: The INACTIVE field in /etc/shadow defines a grace period in days after password expiry during which the user can still log in (but is forced to change the password). If INACTIVE is set to a large number, the user can continue logging in past the expiry date. PAM does enforce shadow expiry by default on standard configurations. chage reads directly from /etc/shadow so they match. SSH key authentication bypasses passwords entirely, but the question implies password login is working.

questions.question: A Linux server needs a process to run at the lowest possible scheduling priority without suspending it. Which command adjusts a running process with PID 1234 to nice value +19?
questions.explanation: renice -n 19 -p 1234 changes the nice value of an already-running process (PID 1234) to +19, the lowest priority. The 'nice' command only sets priority when launching a new process, it cannot modify running processes. 'renice +19 1234' uses an older syntax that may work on some systems but renice -n is the standard POSIX form. nice --adjustment is not valid syntax.

questions.question: After installing a new package, an administrator wants to verify that none of the package's installed files have been modified. The system uses RPM. Which command performs this check?
questions.explanation: rpm -V (verify) compares the installed files of a package against the RPM database, checking size, MD5 hash, permissions, and more. It reports any discrepancies. rpm -qi shows package information (name, version, description). rpm -Vf verifies the package owning a specific file path, not a package name. rpm --checksig verifies the GPG signature of an RPM package file, not installed files.

questions.question: A Debian-based server's apt update fails because a repository key is missing. The key fingerprint is 'ABCD1234'. Which command imports the GPG key from a keyserver?
questions.explanation: apt-key adv passes advanced options to gpg and is the traditional method for importing APT repository keys from a keyserver. apt-key add reads a key from stdin/file but does not fetch from a keyserver. gpg --recv-keys fetches for GPG keyring but not the APT trusted keyring. dpkg --add-key is not a valid dpkg option.

questions.question: A systemd service unit file has 'Type=forking'. The service fails to start and systemctl shows 'Timeout waiting for PID file'. What is the most likely configuration issue?
options: The ExecStart command is incorrect and the service binary is missing
PIDFile= directive is missing or pointing to the wrong path
The service requires Type=simple instead of Type=forking
WantedBy= is not set in the [Install] section
questions.explanation: Type=forking tells systemd that the process forks and the parent exits. systemd then waits for the PID file to appear to confirm startup is complete. If PIDFile= is not set or points to the wrong location, systemd will time out waiting for it. A missing binary would produce 'executable not found', not a PID timeout. Type=simple is for non-forking daemons. WantedBy affects enabling, not startup success.

questions.question: An administrator needs to extend a mounted XFS filesystem on an LVM logical volume after expanding the logical volume with lvextend. Which command resizes the XFS filesystem?
questions.explanation: xfs_growfs takes the mount point (or device) of a mounted XFS filesystem and expands it to fill the available space. XFS can only be grown while mounted, not unmounted. resize2fs is the correct tool for ext2/ext3/ext4, not XFS. xfs_repair -n performs a dry-run check and does not resize. fsck.xfs simply checks the filesystem for damage.

questions.question: An administrator wants to ensure /dev/sdc1 is automatically mounted at /backup at boot, identified by UUID to avoid device naming changes. The filesystem is ext4 and should mount read-only. Which /etc/fstab entry is correct?
questions.explanation: The correct fstab entry uses UUID for stable identification, specifies the mount point /backup, filesystem type ext4, 'ro' for read-only mounting, dump field 0 (no dump), and fsck order 2 (non-root filesystem checked after root). Option A uses 'defaults' which includes rw, not read-only. Option C uses the device path instead of UUID. Option D uses 0 for fsck pass which disables fsck checks on this partition.

questions.question: After running 'useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G wheel devuser', the administrator checks /etc/passwd and sees devuser's primary group is 'devuser', not 'wheel'. Why?
options: The -G flag sets the primary group, which was overridden by useradd defaults
useradd creates a private primary group matching the username by default; -G adds supplementary groups
The wheel group does not exist on this system so useradd fell back to the default group
The -m flag overrides group assignment and creates a new group
questions.explanation: By default, useradd creates a new primary group with the same name as the user (user private group scheme). The -G flag specifies supplementary groups, not the primary group. To set the primary group, you must use -g. So devuser's primary group is 'devuser' and 'wheel' is a supplementary group. If wheel didn't exist, useradd would error, not fall back silently. The -m flag only controls home directory creation.

questions.question: A developer needs to give a script the ability to read files owned by root in /etc/ssl/private without giving the user root access. The script is at /opt/readcert.sh and is owned by root. Which permission configuration achieves this with least privilege?
options: chmod 4755 /opt/readcert.sh to set the SUID bit so it runs as root
Add the developer to the root group and chmod 640 /etc/ssl/private
Create a dedicated group, add both root and the developer to it, and chmod 640 /etc/ssl/private with group ownership
Set sticky bit on /etc/ssl/private with chmod +t
questions.explanation: Creating a dedicated group (e.g., sslreaders), adding the developer's user to it, changing the group ownership of /etc/ssl/private to sslreaders, and setting permissions to 640 or 750 provides access with least privilege. SUID on a shell script is ignored by Linux for security reasons. Adding the developer to the root group grants broad root-group access across the system, violating least privilege. The sticky bit on a directory only affects deletion, not read access.

questions.question: A process is consuming excessive CPU. Running 'ps aux' shows PID 4521 using 98% CPU. The administrator wants to terminate it gracefully first, then forcefully if needed. In what order should signals be sent?
options: SIGKILL (9), then SIGTERM (15) if it persists
SIGTERM (15), then SIGKILL (9) if it does not stop
questions.explanation: The correct order is SIGTERM (15) first, which asks the process to terminate gracefully and allows cleanup handlers to run, then SIGKILL (9) if the process does not respond, which immediately terminates the process without cleanup. SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored, so starting with it skips graceful shutdown. SIGHUP is used to reload configuration in many daemons. SIGSTOP pauses a process but does not terminate it.

questions.question: An administrator wants to prevent a specific kernel module 'pcspkr' from loading at boot. Which method is correct?
questions.explanation: Adding 'blacklist pcspkr' to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/ (such as blacklist.conf) prevents the module from being automatically loaded at boot. This is the persistent, correct method. rmmod removes a currently loaded module but does not prevent future loading. 'install pcspkr /bin/true' is a stronger override (replaces the install command) but is unnecessary for simply blacklisting. /etc/modules is used to load modules at boot, not prevent them.

questions.question: A GRUB2 boot entry fails and the system drops to the GRUB rescue prompt. The administrator types 'ls' and sees '(hd0) (hd0,gpt1) (hd0,gpt2)'. Which sequence of commands boots the system?
options: set root=(hd0,gpt2); linux /vmlinuz root=/dev/sda2; initrd /initrd.img; boot
questions.explanation: From the GRUB rescue prompt, you must set the root device, load the kernel with 'linux', load the initrd, then run 'boot'. The set root command points GRUB to the boot partition. grub-install and update-grub require a running OS. 'insmod normal; normal' is used from the GRUB shell (not rescue) to load the normal module if GRUB modules are available but GRUB's normal mode failed to load.

questions.question: A server running RHEL shows the following in 'journalctl -xe': 'kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 3201 (java) score 890'. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The Java process crashed due to a Java heap space exception in the application
The Linux OOM killer terminated the Java process because the system ran out of available memory
The Java process exceeded its ulimit memory limit and was stopped by the kernel
A cgroup memory limit was reached and the kernel killed the process to enforce the limit
questions.explanation: The OOM (Out of Memory) killer is a kernel mechanism that kills processes when the system has exhausted available memory. The 'score' reflects how aggressively it targets a process (higher = more likely to kill). This is distinct from a Java heap exception (which is a JVM-level error with different log messages), ulimit enforcement (which produces 'Cannot allocate memory' or similar), and cgroup limits (which have different log patterns like 'Memory cgroup limit').

questions.question: After rebooting a system, an administrator notices that a custom service file at /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service has been changed on disk but systemd is still using the old version. What must the administrator run?
questions.explanation: systemctl daemon-reload re-reads all unit files from disk without restarting running services, updating systemd's in-memory configuration. Without it, systemd keeps using the cached version of the unit file. After daemon-reload, restarting the service applies the new configuration. systemctl restart without daemon-reload uses the old unit file. systemctl reload sends SIGHUP to reload the service's own configuration (like nginx -s reload), not the unit file. reset-failed clears failed state flags.

questions.question: An administrator needs to set a file permission of rwxr-x--- (owner: rwx, group: r-x, other: none) using chmod with numeric notation. Which command is correct?
questions.explanation: The permission rwxr-x--- breaks down as: owner (rwx = 4+2+1 = 7), group (r-x = 4+0+1 = 5), other (--- = 0). This gives 750. chmod 754 would set other to r-- (4), adding unwanted read access. chmod 755 sets other to r-x (5). chmod 740 sets group to r-- (4), removing execute from group.

questions.question: A security audit reveals that /etc/passwd is world-writable. Which command fixes this to the correct permissions (readable by all, writable only by root)?
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd should have permissions 644 (rw-r--r--): root can read and write, and all users can read it (many programs need to look up user info). chmod 640 would prevent non-root/non-group users from reading it, breaking many utilities. chmod 600 makes it readable only by root, causing system-wide authentication failures. chmod 444 removes write permission from root, which is also incorrect since root must be able to modify it.

questions.question: An administrator wants to grant user 'bob' read and write ACL access to /srv/project without changing the file's owner or traditional permissions. Which commands achieve this?
questions.explanation: setfacl -m (modify) u:bob:rw /srv/project adds or modifies an ACL entry granting user bob read and write access without affecting ownership or traditional permissions. chown would change ownership. setfacl -x removes ACL entries rather than adding them. getfacl displays ACL entries and does not modify them.

questions.question: An administrator needs to allow the 'developers' group to run 'systemctl restart httpd' as root without a password via sudo. Which /etc/sudoers entry is correct?
questions.explanation: In sudoers, group names are prefixed with %. %developers applies the rule to all members of the developers group. NOPASSWD: allows execution without a password prompt. The command path must be fully qualified. Option A without % applies only to a user named 'developers'. Option C with ALL gives the group all sudo commands, not just the specific one. Option D is missing NOPASSWD:, so it would prompt for a password.

questions.question: A sysadmin needs to harden SSH on a production server. Which /etc/ssh/sshd_config settings are most important to disable password authentication and restrict root logins?
questions.explanation: Setting PasswordAuthentication no disables password-based login (requiring key authentication), and PermitRootLogin no prevents any direct root SSH login. Option A disables passwords but still allows root login. Option B disables key auth (making the server less secure) but does block root. Option D (PermitRootLogin without-password) allows root login via SSH keys, which is generally still discouraged on production systems.

questions.question: An administrator running iptables wants to block all incoming traffic on port 23 (Telnet) from any source. Which command adds the correct rule to the INPUT chain?
questions.explanation: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j DROP appends a rule to the INPUT chain that drops all TCP packets destined for port 23 on this server. --dport specifies the destination port. Using --sport 23 would block traffic from a source port of 23, not incoming connections to port 23. The OUTPUT chain controls outgoing traffic from the server. The FORWARD chain handles traffic being routed through the server, not traffic destined for it.

questions.question: SELinux is in enforcing mode and a web application cannot write to /var/app/uploads even though the directory permissions are 777. What is the most likely cause and correct fix?
options: The directory needs chmod 1777 to set the sticky bit for shared writes
The SELinux file context on /var/app/uploads is wrong; run 'chcon -t httpd_sys_rw_content_t /var/app/uploads'
The httpd process is running as the wrong user; fix with 'usermod -aG apache www-data'
SELinux boolean httpd_can_network_connect needs to be enabled with 'setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on'
questions.explanation: SELinux enforcing mode enforces mandatory access controls based on file contexts. Even with permissions 777, if the SELinux context is wrong (e.g., default_t instead of httpd_sys_rw_content_t), the web server process will be denied. chcon changes the context immediately. For a permanent fix, restorecon or semanage fcontext should also be used. The sticky bit affects deletion, not writes. The boolean httpd_can_network_connect relates to network access, not filesystem writes.

questions.question: An administrator notices multiple failed sudo attempts in /var/log/auth.log for user 'mallory'. Which journalctl command filters only authentication failures for this user?
questions.explanation: journalctl _COMM=sudo filters journal entries where the command is 'sudo', then piping through grep -i mallory finds entries related to that user. This is a structured journal field query. Option A searches the sudo unit which may not exist (sudo is typically not a systemd unit). Option C shows recent context but doesn't filter by user. journalctl -f /var/log/auth.log is invalid syntax — you cannot specify both -f and a log file path; journalctl reads from the journal, not files.

questions.question: A developer generates a GPG key pair and wants to encrypt a file 'report.txt' for a colleague whose public key is already imported in the GPG keyring with email 'colleague@example.com'. Which command is correct?
questions.explanation: gpg --encrypt -r colleague@example.com report.txt encrypts the file using the recipient's public key. Only the holder of the corresponding private key can decrypt it. --sign creates a digital signature to verify authenticity but does not encrypt. --decrypt is used to decrypt a file, not encrypt. --gen-key generates a new key pair and does not take email/file arguments this way.

questions.question: AppArmor is installed and a profile exists for /usr/sbin/nginx. The administrator wants to put the profile in complain mode for testing without enforcement. Which command is correct?
questions.explanation: aa-complain switches an AppArmor profile to complain mode, where policy violations are logged but not blocked — ideal for testing. setenforce 0 is an SELinux command, not AppArmor. aa-enforce switches a profile to enforcing mode. apparmor_parser -R removes (unloads) the profile entirely rather than setting a mode.

questions.question: A Bash script contains the following code: `for f in *.log; do gzip $f; done`. The script runs but some filenames with spaces cause errors. How should the variable be quoted to fix this?
options: for f in *.log; do gzip '$f'; done
for f in *.log; do gzip "$f"; done
for f in "*.log"; do gzip $f; done
for f in *.log; do gzip ${f}; done
questions.explanation: Double-quoting "$f" ensures that filenames with spaces are treated as a single argument to gzip. Single quotes '$f' would pass the literal string '$f' rather than the variable value. Quoting the glob "*.log" prevents shell expansion, so no files would be found. ${f} (without quotes) still performs word splitting on spaces and does not fix the problem.

questions.question: A Bash script exits with code 127. What does this exit code specifically indicate?
options: The script was killed by an external signal (SIGTERM)
The script ran successfully but returned an error from an internal function
A command in the script was not found (command not found error)
The script exceeded its allowed execution time
questions.explanation: Exit code 127 in Bash means 'command not found' — the shell could not locate the executable being called. This is typically caused by a typo in the command name, a missing PATH entry, or a missing binary. Exit code 130 or 143 indicate signal termination. Internal function errors return whatever the function explicitly returns. There is no standard exit code for timeout (timeout command sends SIGTERM = 124).

questions.question: An administrator needs to extract only the third field (colon-delimited) from /etc/passwd to list all usernames. Which command is correct?
questions.explanation: Usernames are in the FIRST field of /etc/passwd. cut -d: -f1 uses colon as delimiter and extracts field 1 (the username). cut -d: -f3 extracts the UID (third field). awk -F: '{print $1}' also extracts the username correctly — but note that option A would be correct for usernames too, while the question asks which of the given commands lists usernames. sed -n '3p' prints the third line of the file, not a field.

questions.question: A Bash script must check if a file exists before processing it. Which conditional expression is correct?
questions.explanation: [ -f /etc/config.file ] tests if the path exists AND is a regular file (not a directory or special file). -d tests for a directory, which is wrong for a file. The combination -e (exists) and -x (executable) checks existence and executability, which is not what 'processing a file' generally requires. The test with -r and -w checks read and write permissions, which is more than just 'exists'.

questions.question: A script needs to count how many times the word 'ERROR' appears in /var/log/app.log. Which command produces only the count?
options: All of the above produce the same output
questions.explanation: grep -c ERROR /var/log/app.log prints only the count of matching lines directly. grep | wc -l also counts matching lines but requires a pipe. awk counts matching lines too but with more verbosity. While A and B produce the same count for line occurrences, option D is incorrect because awk counts differently if a line has multiple occurrences of ERROR (it counts the line once). grep -c is the most concise single-command solution.

questions.question: An administrator needs to replace every occurrence of 'localhost' with '127.0.0.1' in /etc/myapp.conf in place. Which sed command is correct?
questions.explanation: sed -i 's/localhost/127.0.0.1/g' modifies the file in place (-i) and the 'g' flag replaces ALL occurrences on each line. Without -i, sed outputs to stdout and does not modify the file. Without 'g', only the first occurrence per line is replaced. Option D uses incorrect sed syntax (missing 's' substitution command prefix).

questions.question: A developer initializes a new git repository and stages all files with 'git add .'. Before committing, they want to see exactly what changes are staged. Which command shows the staged diff?
questions.explanation: git diff --cached (also known as git diff --staged) shows the difference between the staging area (index) and the last commit — i.e., what will be included in the next commit. git diff without flags shows unstaged changes (working directory vs. staging area), which would be empty for newly staged files. git status --short shows file states but not the actual content diff. git log --stat shows commit history, not staged changes.

questions.question: A team wants to create a feature branch named 'feature/auth' from main and switch to it in one command. Which git command achieves this?
options: git branch feature/auth && git checkout feature/auth
questions.explanation: git checkout -b feature/auth creates a new branch named feature/auth and switches to it in a single command, equivalent to running git branch and git checkout separately. git switch feature/auth switches to an existing branch but does not create it (git switch -c would create it). git clone --branch checks out an existing remote branch from a repository, not creating a local feature branch.

questions.question: A Dockerfile is being written for a Python web application. The requirements.txt is copied and dependencies are installed first, before copying the application code. Why is this ordering important?
options: Python's pip requires requirements.txt before application code can be parsed
Docker caches each layer; copying requirements first ensures the dependency install layer is cached when only app code changes
The COPY instruction fails if application files are copied before requirements.txt
The FROM instruction requires dependencies to be declared before application code
questions.explanation: Docker builds images layer by layer and caches each layer. If requirements.txt changes infrequently but application code changes often, placing the COPY requirements.txt and RUN pip install before COPY . ensures that Docker reuses the cached dependency layer when only app code changes, dramatically speeding up builds. This is a fundamental Docker build optimization. pip does not require this ordering at a technical level, and COPY does not fail based on ordering.

questions.question: An administrator runs a container with 'docker run -d -v /host/data:/container/data:ro nginx'. What does the ':ro' flag specify?
options: The container runs in read-only (restricted operations) mode
The bind mount /host/data is mounted read-only inside the container
The nginx image is pulled from a read-only registry
The container filesystem is immutable and cannot write to any path
questions.explanation: In Docker volume syntax, the :ro suffix mounts the specific bind mount as read-only inside the container. The container can read files from /host/data but cannot write to it. This only affects this specific mount, not the container's writable layer or other paths. 'Read-only container mode' (docker run --read-only) is a separate flag. The :ro has no relation to registry access.

questions.question: A cron job must run a backup script every day at 2:30 AM. Which crontab entry is correct?
questions.explanation: Cron fields are: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. '30 2 * * *' means minute 30, hour 2, every day of month, every month, every day of week — i.e., 2:30 AM daily. Option B swaps minute and hour. Option C has the values in wrong positions (day 2, minute 30). Option D runs at 2:00 AM only on the 30th of each month.

questions.question: An Ansible playbook task needs to install the 'nginx' package on Debian-based hosts and ensure it is the latest version. Which task definition is correct?
options:
- name: Install nginx
  yum:
    name: nginx
    state: latest

- name: Install nginx
  apt:
    name: nginx
    state: latest
    update_cache: yes

- name: Install nginx
  package:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Install nginx
  apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present
questions.explanation: The apt module is correct for Debian-based systems. state: latest ensures the most recent version is installed. update_cache: yes runs apt-get update before installing, ensuring fresh package information. The yum module is for Red Hat/CentOS. The generic 'package' module with state: present installs but does not guarantee the latest version. apt with state: present installs but only ensures the package exists, not that it is the latest version.

questions.question: A Bash function is defined to check connectivity and return 0 on success or 1 on failure. How should the exit code of the function be captured in a script variable?
questions.explanation: In Bash, $? holds the exit status (return code) of the last command or function. Calling check_connectivity; result=$? runs the function and captures its return code in result. Option A captures stdout output of the function, not the exit code. Option C is invalid Bash syntax. Option D exports result before the function runs, which does not capture the return value.

questions.question: A server shows a load average of '18.5 14.2 9.8' in top. The system has 4 CPU cores. What does this indicate?
options: The system is healthy; load averages above 10 are normal for any server
The system is severely overloaded; there are far more runnable processes than CPU cores can handle
The system had a brief spike 15 minutes ago and is now recovering, as shown by the decreasing trend
The load represents memory usage in gigabytes, not CPU load
questions.explanation: Load average represents the average number of runnable (or uninterruptible) processes over 1, 5, and 15 minutes. On a 4-core system, a load of 1.0 per core (4.0 total) means fully utilized. A load of 18.5 at 1 minute means 4.6x overload — the system is severely overloaded with many processes waiting for CPU. Option C is partially true (the trend is decreasing) but does not address the severity. Load average measures process queue depth, not memory.

questions.question: An administrator suspects network issues and wants to capture all TCP traffic on interface eth0 on port 443 to a file for later analysis. Which tcpdump command is correct?
questions.explanation: tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap tcp port 443 captures TCP traffic on port 443 on interface eth0 and writes raw packets to a pcap file for analysis with Wireshark or tcpdump -r. Option A captures to stdout but does not save to file. Option C uses incorrect filter syntax (tcp:443 is not valid; it should be 'tcp port 443') and redirecting tcpdump stdout captures text output, not binary pcap. tcpdump does not use --interface or --write as long options.

questions.question: After a kernel update, an administrator attempts to boot but sees 'Kernel panic - not syncing: VFS: Unable to mount root fs'. The most likely cause is:
options: The GRUB bootloader configuration points to the wrong kernel version
The new kernel's initramfs is missing or does not contain the storage driver needed to mount root
The root filesystem has a journal error that can be fixed with fsck
The /etc/fstab entry for the root filesystem uses an incorrect UUID
questions.explanation: The initramfs (initial RAM filesystem) contains the minimal drivers and tools needed to mount the root filesystem during early boot. If the initramfs for the new kernel is missing or does not include the storage controller driver (e.g., a SCSI or NVMe driver), the kernel cannot find and mount the root device. Wrong GRUB kernel pointer would either boot the old kernel or show a different error. A filesystem journal error causes different messages. An incorrect UUID in fstab would cause issues after root is mounted, not prevent VFS mount.

questions.question: A system with SELinux in enforcing mode was cloned from another server. On first boot, files have incorrect SELinux contexts. The administrator needs to trigger a full filesystem relabeling on next reboot. Which command creates the required trigger file?
questions.explanation: Creating the file /.autorelabel causes the SELinux subsystem to perform a full filesystem relabeling on the next reboot, then remove the file and reboot again. This is the standard method after cloning or major context changes. restorecon -Rv / would attempt relabeling on a live system but may miss some files if the filesystem is busy. semanage fcontext adds policy rules but doesn't trigger relabeling. fixfiles -F onboot is an alternative method but touch /.autorelabel is the most widely documented standard approach.

questions.question: A disk shows 95% usage but 'df -h' shows the filesystem is 60% full. What is the most likely cause?
options: The filesystem was mounted with the 'noatime' option which skews usage reporting
Inode exhaustion — the filesystem has run out of inodes even though block space is available
There are large files deleted but still held open by running processes, so space is not reclaimed
LVM thin provisioning is reporting available physical space, not logical space
questions.explanation: Each file requires an inode. If a filesystem runs out of inodes (even with block space remaining), no new files can be created. df -h shows block usage but df -i shows inode usage. When df -i shows 100% but df -h shows 60%, inode exhaustion is the cause. Deleted files held open (option C) would show high block usage on df -h. noatime affects access time updates, not usage reporting. LVM thin provisioning discrepancies would show in different vgs/lvs output.

questions.question: An administrator uses 'ip route show' and sees 'default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0'. When they try to reach an external server, connections time out. 'ping 192.168.1.1' succeeds. What should the administrator check next?
options: Run 'systemctl restart networking' to refresh routes
Check if the default gateway 192.168.1.1 has internet connectivity and if NAT or firewall rules are blocking outbound traffic
Add a static route with 'ip route add 0.0.0.0/0 via 192.168.1.1'
The MTU on eth0 may be incorrect; run 'ip link set eth0 mtu 1500'
questions.explanation: The local routing is correct (default gateway is reachable). Since ping to 192.168.1.1 works but external connectivity fails, the problem is upstream from the server: the gateway may lack internet access, or NAT/firewall rules may be blocking outbound traffic. restarting networking won't help since routes are already correct. ip route add 0.0.0.0/0 is redundant since a default route already exists. MTU issues would cause partial connectivity or large packet drops, not complete timeouts from a single hop away.

questions.question: A Linux server's /var partition is 100% full, causing application failures. The administrator identifies large rotated logs in /var/log. Which sequence of commands frees space and prevents recurrence?
options: find /var/log -name '*.gz' -mtime +30 -delete && configure logrotate to limit log size
questions.explanation: Finding and deleting compressed rotated log archives older than 30 days removes old data without risking active log files, then configuring logrotate with size limits prevents recurrence. rm -rf /var/log/* is dangerous as it removes active log files and directory structure. Truncating syslog only frees space from one file without addressing root cause. Bind mounting /tmp to /var/log would hide existing logs and is not a real solution.

questions.question: A systemd service 'webapp' keeps failing. Running 'systemctl status webapp' shows 'Active: failed (Result: exit-code)'. Which command shows the detailed failure reason from the service's log output?
questions.explanation: journalctl -u webapp -n 50 shows the last 50 journal entries for the webapp unit, including the process's stdout/stderr output which reveals why it exited with an error. The service may not write to /var/log/webapp.log at all if it's logging to stdout (captured by systemd journal). systemctl show displays unit properties/parameters in machine-readable format, not service output. dmesg shows kernel ring buffer messages, not application logs.

questions.question: A user reports they cannot log in with their password. The administrator checks /etc/shadow and sees the account entry as: 'alice:!$6$hash...:19000:0:90:7:::'. What does the '!' prefix on the password hash indicate?
options: The account requires two-factor authentication before the password is validated
The account password is locked — logins using this password will be rejected
The password field uses a different hashing algorithm than SHA-512
The account has never had a password set and the field is empty
questions.explanation: A '!' (exclamation mark) prepended to the password hash in /etc/shadow locks the account by making the hash invalid. Authentication will fail because no password can produce a hash matching '!hash'. This is what usermod -L does. Two-factor authentication is configured via PAM, not shadow file markers. The hash algorithm is indicated by the $6$ prefix (SHA-512) regardless of the leading !. An unset password would have an empty field or a single '*'.

questions.question: An administrator needs to troubleshoot why a network service is not listening on port 8080. Which command shows all listening TCP sockets with the associated process name?
questions.explanation: ss -tlnp shows TCP (-t) listening (-l) sockets with numeric ports (-n) and the process name/PID (-p). This confirms whether anything is bound to port 8080. netstat -a shows all connections but not just listening, and netstat is deprecated in favor of ss. lsof -i :8080 is also valid but the question asks for the tool showing listening sockets with process info in a compact format. ip link show displays network interface information, not socket states.

questions.question: A server's performance is slow. Running 'vmstat 1 5' shows consistently high 'wa' values around 80%. What does this indicate?
options: The system's swap usage is extremely high and pages are being swapped to disk
The CPUs are waiting for I/O operations to complete — disk is the bottleneck
The network interface is saturated and causing packet wait times
80% of CPU time is being used by user-space processes
questions.explanation: In vmstat output, 'wa' (iowait) represents the percentage of CPU time spent waiting for I/O operations (typically disk) to complete. High wa (>20-30%) indicates the disk is the bottleneck. Swap activity is shown in the 'si' (swap in) and 'so' (swap out) columns. Network saturation is not directly shown by vmstat wa. CPU user-space time is shown in the 'us' column.

questions.question: An administrator is rebuilding initramfs after installing a new storage driver on a RHEL/CentOS system. Which command regenerates initramfs for the currently running kernel?
questions.explanation: On RHEL/CentOS systems, dracut is the initramfs generator. 'dracut --force' regenerates the initramfs, overwriting the existing one. The --force flag is needed when the file already exists. update-initramfs -u is the Debian/Ubuntu equivalent (uses initramfs-tools). mkinitrd is the older legacy tool replaced by dracut on modern RHEL. grub2-mkconfig regenerates GRUB configuration, not initramfs.

questions.question: A developer's Dockerfile has 'CMD ["python", "app.py"]' and the container is started with 'docker run myimage python debug.py'. What actually runs?
options: Both app.py and debug.py run in parallel within the container
python debug.py — the run command arguments override CMD
python app.py — CMD cannot be overridden at runtime
An error occurs because conflicting commands cannot be resolved
questions.explanation: CMD in a Dockerfile specifies the default command to run, but it is overridden by arguments passed to 'docker run' after the image name. So 'docker run myimage python debug.py' runs 'python debug.py' instead. ENTRYPOINT (not CMD) is harder to override and is typically used for fixed commands. CMD is designed to be overridable defaults. No error occurs — this is expected behavior.

questions.question: An administrator needs to view all DNS records for the domain 'example.com', including MX and TXT records. Which command retrieves all record types?
questions.explanation: dig example.com ANY queries for ALL DNS record types associated with the domain. nslookup example.com by default only queries for A records. host -a does query for all records and is a valid alternative, but dig is the standard tool for detailed DNS investigation and is preferred in exam contexts. ping -a does DNS resolution but only retrieves the A record for ICMP testing purposes.

questions.question: A production system's GRUB2 boot menu shows two kernel entries. The older kernel is currently booting. An administrator wants to permanently set the newer kernel as the default. After updating /etc/default/grub with GRUB_DEFAULT=0, what must be run?
questions.explanation: After modifying /etc/default/grub, grub2-mkconfig regenerates the active grub.cfg from the templates in /etc/grub.d/ and the settings in /etc/default/grub. Without running this command, grub.cfg is unchanged and the setting has no effect. systemctl reboot just reboots without updating GRUB. grub2-install reinstalls the GRUB bootloader to the MBR/EFI partition, which is not needed here. update-grub is a Debian/Ubuntu wrapper equivalent to grub2-mkconfig but uses different output path syntax.

questions.question: A Podman container must run a long-running data processing job and continue after the user logs out. The container is named 'dataproc'. Which command ensures the container keeps running after logout?
questions.explanation: podman run --detach (-d) runs the container in the background, detached from the terminal. The container process runs under the Podman system, not tied to the user's shell session, so it persists after logout. --restart always is a Docker concept; in rootless Podman, auto-restart requires systemd unit files or podman generate systemd. nohup and disown are shell techniques to detach processes from terminal sessions but are not the clean Podman-native approach.

questions.question: A script is failing intermittently in production. To debug it, an administrator wants to trace every command executed and its expanded value. Which bash invocation enables this tracing?
questions.explanation: bash -x runs a script in trace mode, printing each command after parameter expansion and before execution, prefixed with '+'. This shows the actual values of variables and the exact commands being run. bash -e causes the script to exit immediately on any error but does not show trace output. bash -v prints lines as they are read (before expansion), which is less useful for debugging. bash -n parses the script for syntax errors without executing it.
